candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Agent and appraiser relativism remain distinct even when one person occupies both roles, because the views index moral evaluation differently.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn begins with an explicit affirmative response to McAllister's question and develops Bush's previously introduced distinction.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move directly defends a conceptual distinction that underlies Bush's broader challenge to common realist treatments of relativism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: McAllister's claim that agent and appraiser relativism collapse into a mere change of perspective.

candidates.contextSummary: McAllister had argued that agents commonly appraise their own conduct, making the distinction seem epistemic rather than ontological; Bush answers by separating the relevant standards of evaluation.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Agent relativism generates conflicting obligations when different agents or cultures authorize incompatible actions and demands.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted explanatory turn continues Bush's response and uses wallet-taking and cultural-intervention cases to expose conflicts.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The conflict argument supplies a substantive reason that agent relativism has normative difficulties beyond merely changing evaluative perspective.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: McAllister's suggestion that agent and appraiser relativism differ only rhetorically or perspectivally.

candidates.contextSummary: After distinguishing the two forms of relativism, Bush tests agent relativism with clashes between agents' standards and between cultures' opposing prescriptions.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Appraiser relativism reduces moral assertions to perspective-indexed descriptive content without imposing the agent relativist's external normative obligations.
candidates.attributionBasis: Bush explicitly contrasts appraiser relativism with the conflict cases he has just developed for agent relativism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This contrast explains why objections based on conflicting obligations target agent relativism but do not transfer to appraiser relativism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: McAllister's proposed collapse of appraiser relativism into the same practical position as agent relativism.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush argues that an appraiser can recognize another culture's approval as a descriptive fact while remaining free to oppose, assist, or ignore its practice.

candidates.speaker: Derek McAllister
candidates.proposition: The agent-appraiser distinction is rhetorically and epistemically useful, but its deeper significance may amount only to perspective and resulting implications.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly shifts to classroom experience and restates McAllister's concern about the limited value of the distinction.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move preserves McAllister's main objection after Bush's examples by conceding pedagogical utility while denying a deeper categorical difference.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Bush's argument that agent and appraiser relativism differ substantively in their normative structure.

candidates.contextSummary: McAllister acknowledges that perspective labels help students track evaluation, yet maintains that both positions remain relativist and may differ chiefly in consequences.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Appraiser relativism is a genuine metaethical position with semantic and metaphysical commitments, not merely descriptive variation among moral practices.
candidates.attributionBasis: Bush begins with an explicit clarification and distinguishes descriptive relativism from appraiser relativism's semantic and metaphysical theses.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move bears directly on whether anti-realist alternatives are conceptually substantive and on how the realism-versus-anti-realism framing should be understood.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: McAllister's characterization of the appraiser-agent contrast as little more than a perspective switch.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush locates appraiser relativism alongside other analytic metaethical theories, while criticizing the standard discourse and favoring irreducible normativity as a more useful divide.

candidates.speaker: Derek McAllister
candidates.proposition: Even when both views are properly metaethical, agent and appraiser relativism may remain versions of one underlying relativism differentiated by perspective.
candidates.attributionBasis: McAllister explicitly clarifies his earlier wording and develops an extended perspectival analogy before asking whether his interpretation is correct.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move refines rather than abandons the collapse objection, conceding metaethical status while disputing the depth of the distinction.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Bush's clarification that appraiser relativism has genuine semantic and metaphysical metaethical content.

candidates.contextSummary: McAllister uses the varying manifestation of a single vice across perspectives as an analogy for two relativist views that retain one basic identity despite practical differences.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Agent relativism has realist-like externally binding implications, whereas appraiser relativism removes such external imposition and is therefore practically distinct.
candidates.attributionBasis: Bush directly answers McAllister's question and systematically contrasts the semantic content and normative commitments of the two views.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument identifies a concrete normative difference that rebuts the claim that the positions are merely alternate perspectives on one view.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: McAllister's analogy suggesting that the two forms of relativism share one identity despite perspectival manifestations.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush describes agent relativism as allowing others' values to create obligations binding on an individual, while appraiser relativism leaves conduct unconstrained by outside standards.

candidates.speaker: Derek McAllister
candidates.proposition: Agent relativism may still collapse toward appraiser relativism because any external culture's standards bind an agent only through that agent's own understanding.
candidates.attributionBasis: McAllister acknowledges Bush's explanation and then introduces a distinct epistemic route to his continuing collapse argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move responds to Bush's normative contrast by arguing that first-person epistemic mediation restores a significant structural similarity between the positions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Bush's claim that agent relativism uniquely imposes other people's or cultures' standards on the individual.

candidates.contextSummary: McAllister argues that an agent can encounter another culture's supposedly binding code only as interpreted from within the agent's own perspective.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Epistemic mediation is not distinctive to agent relativism and does not falsify it, since moral realists face comparable access limitations.
candidates.attributionBasis: Bush immediately rejects the proposed distinctive problem, compares realism's epistemic access, and warns against consequence-based rejection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply neutralizes McAllister's revised collapse argument and separates epistemic difficulty from evidence that a metaethical position is false.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: McAllister's argument that first-person interpretation makes agent relativism resemble appraiser relativism.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush maintains that every metaethical view must address limited access to relevant facts or standards and cautions that undesirable consequences do not establish falsity.

candidates.speaker: Lance Bush
candidates.proposition: Persistent expert misunderstanding of anti-realism weakens confidence that historical speakers reliably held moral realism or clearly grasped the relevant distinction.
candidates.attributionBasis: Bush explicitly returns to his original historical point and supports it with examples of contemporary realists misunderstanding preference-based anti-realism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The inference directly addresses the claimed historical and common-sense advantage of realism by challenging reliable attribution of realism to earlier thinkers.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The earlier realist appeal to historical prevalence and to ordinary or traditional understanding of moral realism.

candidates.contextSummary: Bush argues that even trained contemporary philosophers sometimes fail to understand why subjective preferences can matter, making confident realist readings of less-equipped historical people doubtful.
